strings.name: Ben Bernanke
strings.summary: Ben Bernanke studied how bank failures deepened the Great Depression and brought financial history into central banking. As Federal Reserve chair from 2006 to 2014, he helped respond to the global financial crisis with emergency lending, near-zero interest rates and asset purchases, policies that also drew criticism. He shared the 2022 economics prize with Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig and continued research on monetary policy and institutional governance after leaving office.
strings.coverageNote: Checked through 13 November 2026; selected events reach his July 2026 governance appointment. Fed policy involved collective decisions. The prize recognized academic research, not every policy of his chairmanship.
strings.influence.rationale: Researched banking crises and the Great Depression and led the Federal Reserve during the global financial crisis.
strings.facts.fact-01.label: Birth and upbringing
strings.facts.fact-01.value: Born in Augusta, Georgia; raised in Dillon, South Carolina
strings.facts.fact-02.label: Education
strings.facts.fact-02.value: BA in economics, Harvard University (1975); PhD in economics, MIT (1979)
strings.highlights.highlight-01.title: Explaining banks and crises
strings.highlights.highlight-01.text: His Great Depression research showed how damage to credit intermediation can worsen an economic downturn, contributing to the 2022 economics prize.
strings.highlights.highlight-02.title: Central banking during a crisis
strings.highlights.highlight-02.text: Led emergency Fed measures during the financial crisis; these helped stabilize banks while provoking debate over central-bank authority and risk.
strings.timeline.event-01.title: Joins an AI governance trust
strings.timeline.event-01.text: Anthropic announced his appointment to its Long-Term Benefit Trust, an independent body with authority to appoint company directors.
strings.timeline.event-02.title: Publishes a Bank of England review
strings.timeline.event-02.text: Completed an independent review with twelve recommendations on forecasting infrastructure, policymaking and public communication.
strings.timeline.event-03.title: Shares the economics prize
strings.timeline.event-03.text: Received the prize with Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig for research on banks and financial crises.
strings.timeline.event-04.title: Ends his term as Fed chair
strings.timeline.event-04.text: His chairmanship ended in January; he subsequently moved into research at Brookings and continued work on monetary policy.
strings.timeline.event-05.title: Responds to the global financial crisis
strings.timeline.event-05.text: The Fed introduced emergency lending and asset purchases and cut rates sharply; bank stabilization measures also drew fierce criticism.
strings.timeline.event-06.title: Becomes Federal Reserve chair
strings.timeline.event-06.text: Moved from chairing the Council of Economic Advisers to the Fed, beginning the first of two terms.
strings.timeline.event-07.title: Joins the Federal Reserve Board
strings.timeline.event-07.text: Moved from Princeton into public service and served as a Fed governor until 2005.
strings.timeline.event-08.title: Joins Princeton University
strings.timeline.event-08.text: After Stanford, became a professor of economics and public affairs, later chairing the department and studying monetary and financial history.
strings.timeline.event-09.title: Earns an economics doctorate
strings.timeline.event-09.text: Completed his PhD at MIT and began teaching at Stanford Graduate School of Business.
strings.timeline.event-10.title: Graduates from Harvard
strings.timeline.event-10.text: Earned a BA in economics before pursuing graduate research in macroeconomics and financial crises.
strings.timeline.event-11.title: Born in Augusta
strings.timeline.event-11.text: Born in Georgia and spent his childhood and teenage years in Dillon, South Carolina.
